findings.description: Raising the public error after leaving the internal except blocks removes internal exception context in ordinary calls, but does not guarantee the required absence of context. If a caller invokes a validator while handling another exception, Python assigns that caller's active exception to the new error's __context__. 'from None' suppresses its display but does not remove the context object, which can retain sensitive caller exception data. Existing tests exercise only calls without an ambient exception.
findings.remedy: Resolve the strict no-context contract for calls made inside an active exception handler, and add a regression assertion covering a caller exception containing a planted synthetic secret. Do not equate suppressed traceback display with absent exception context.

findings.description: The public error does not always satisfy the required absence of exception context. If a validator is called while its caller is handling another exception, raising DeletionProtocolError(code) from None still attaches that active exception as __context__. The explicit cause is null and ordinary traceback display is suppressed, but programmatic exception inspection can recover the caller exception and any sensitive text it contains. Raising outside the local except blocks only prevents attachment of the locally caught validation exception. Existing tests invoke validators without an active caller exception, so they miss this case.
findings.remedy: Ensure the public boundary delivers errors with both __context__ and __cause__ actually null, including when invoked inside an existing exception handler. Add a regression with a synthetic-secret-bearing caller exception and inspect the resulting error attributes, not only its displayed string.
